entry.title: Stop Using Docker In Production — Here's Why
entry.summary:
Docker has become the default for deploying applications. But here's the uncomfortable truth: most teams are using Docker wrong, and it's costing them time, money, and sanity. Docker was designed for microservices at scale. Yet teams with 3 developers and a single monolith are containerizing everything. The result? 30-minute build times for a simple PHP app 17 layers of abstraction between you and your code Docker Compose files longer than your actual application Network debugging that requires a PhD in overlay drivers Let me be clear: Docker solves real problems. But only specific ones: Multi-service architectures with 5+ independent services Cross-team environments where consistent runtime matters CI/CD pipelines that need reproducible builds Local development for complex stacks (databases, caches, queues) For everything else, you're paying a tax:
Scenario Docker Overhead Alternative
Single Python API High venv + systemd
Static frontend Extreme nginx + CDN
PHP monolith High PHP-FPM + nginx
Small team (<5 devs) Medium Direct deployment
Every layer of abstraction has a cost. Docker adds: Debugging complexity (logs, networking, volumes) Build time (image layers, caching, registry) Security surface (container escapes, vulnerable base images) Cognitive load (when did your team last read Docker docs?) Start simple. Deploy directly to a VPS first. Add Docker only when you feel the pain. Not before. Use Docker for development, not production. Local consistency ≠ production complexity. If you must container, use distroless images. Fewer layers = fewer problems. Docker is a tool, not a religion. The best engineers I know use the simplest solution that works. Sometimes that's Docker. Often it's not. Stop containerizing everything. Start thinking about what you're actually solving. What's your Docker horror story? I've got a whole folder of docker-compose.yml files I'd love to burn.
